doc.title: Dick Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

title: Technology, drugs, his children and Monk's background
summary: Compares college then and now: no television before 1952, no drugs; his son and daughter attended Hamilton; talk turns to Monk's daughter and job.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Do you think the learning process has changed a lot due to technology? © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
Oh sure. We were pretty primitive. Remember I said that we didn’t get television until 1952 let alone computers. Nobody ever thought what a computer —
Right. And cell phones.

Oh no, no, no. We didn’t know what it was. But on the good side we didn’t have any drugs. Nobody even knew what marijuana was. We would get pretty drunk on booze but we didn’t need any, didn’t have any drugs, didn’t need any drugs, didn’t want any drugs. My son was a Hamilton graduate, class of ’78, and he said he smoked pot all the time here.
Uh huh. Did you have another one too?
Yeah I have a daughter, Wendy, class of ’85. My son is the class of ’78, my daughter is the class of ’85. And by that time there was a lot of drugs.
Uh huh. Well my daughter just graduated from here also.
Good, congratulations Monk.
So we’re very happy.
Oh good, I’m glad. Yes.
So it’s interesting for me because growing up I did not know about Hamilton but I certainly do now.
Where did you come from?
From Rochester.
Okay.
But I ended up in this area and this has been a great experience meeting all my jazz heroes through this project.
It’s a great experience for Hamilton to have you, and being a player, I think that is so inspirational.
Well thank you.
To look up there on the stage and there you are.
Well it helps talking to musicians.
Oh yes, oh yes, sure.
